title: Wall Street bulls are starting to admit the earnings bubble is real—and the 60/40 portfolio may be the first casualty
description: Goldman’s chief global equity strategist Peter Oppenheimer said, “There does not appear to be a valuation bubble, but there may be an earnings bubble.”
fullText:
For more than four decades, the investing world operated on a foundational assumption: that a portfolio consisting of 60% stocks and 40% bonds would protect you when markets turned. For roughly the past 20 years, a second assumption took hold alongside it: that a handful of dominant tech companies would keep growing into whatever price investors were willing to pay. This has taken on several shapes, with the FAANG companies morphing into the "Magnificent Seven" during the pandemic, and the AI boom crowning a new group of "hyperscalers."

But these assumptions are taking a hit from sources that rarely deliver bad news about the markets they cover.

Goldman Sachs, one of the Street's most consistently bullish research shops, published a note Monday authored by chief global equity strategist Peter Oppenheimer conceding that "there does not appear to be a valuation bubble, but there may be an earnings bubble" in the technology sector.

The same day, Apollo chief economist Torsten Slok wrote in his Daily Spark note that "the 60/40 portfolio is broken," arguing that with the AI trade slowing down and government debt projected to reach 175% of GDP, "neither the 60 nor the 40 responds to what made it work in the first place."

Both notes came after a week of Big Tech earnings that saw shockingly large moves both up and down for major tech firms, with analysts debating whether they reflected the true shape of the AI moat or "financial nihilism."

Microsoft made history with a 17% stock surge, adding nearly $500 billion in market capitalization in one day, its largest single-day move since the financial crisis year of 2008. In fact, Oppenheimer said Monday that the market is seeing things change in a way they haven't since the Great Recession.

The 60/40 rule wasn't always gospel. Its theoretical roots trace to Harry Markowitz's 1952 work on portfolio theory, but it only became institutional orthodoxy during the four-decade stretch of falling interest rates that began in the early 1980s. That decline let bonds do double duty as both income and ballast against equities, a dynamic that market analysts have called the "golden age" of investing.

Slok's warning isn't a reaction to one bad earnings season. He has argued since at least 2023 that rates would stay "higher for longer" than consensus expected. By late May 2026, he had sharpened that macro call into a specific yield-curve mechanism: Front-end rates were rising on sticky inflation; the middle of the curve was under pressure "because of hyperscaler issuance"; and long-end rates were climbing on "more Treasury supply and less Fed demand." His Aug. 3 argument that "the real risk emerges if the AI trade reverses or markets become more worried about government deficits" is a continuation of that multiyear thesis, not a new one.

title: Apple challenges UK government's latest demand for iCloud backdoor: report
description: Apple has appealed a new legal demand by the U.K. government, which critics say could threaten the privacy rights of users all over the world.
fullText:
Apple is challenging another legal demand by the U.K. government to access the encrypted data of its users in the country, according to the Financial Times.

The company reportedly filed a complaint with the U.K.’s Investigatory Powers Tribunal, a court that hears cases related to government surveillance, after the government last year issued a “technical capability notice”. The notice is a secret government legal order for demanding access to users’ data, even if the data is encrypted.

For critics, this kind of demand is the equivalent of requesting a backdoor into Apple’s cloud backups that have Advanced Data Protection (ADP) switched on, which makes the data end-to-end encrypted and inaccessible to anyone other than the customer, including to Apple.

This new challenge comes a year after a similar fight between Apple and the U.K. government. In early 2025, London issued a secret order to Apple demanding access to users’ encrypted iCloud backups, which was later dropped following the intervention of the Trump administration.

After the first order, the company reacted by removing the ability of U.K. users to use ADP. Then, in October, the U.K. issued a second order, which Apple is now challenging.

Apple did not respond to TechCrunch’s request for comment.

title: Ireland 'laser-focused' on World Cup qualification
description: Ireland's five-game ODI series against Afghanistan this week marks the start of their preparations for next year's World Cup qualifying tournament.
fullText:
As he prepares to take charge of Ireland for the first time in a five-game ODI series against Afghanistan starting on Wednesday, new head coach Gary Wilson has challenged the side to make their own World Cup history.

Ireland have not qualified for the 50-over competition since 2015 but, as they return to the format for the first time in 15 months this week, Wilson says his squad are "laser-focused" on making it to South Africa, Zimbabwe and Namibia next autumn.

Wilson played in that tournament 11 years ago, and four years prior when the side famously toppled England in Bangalore (now Bengaluru), so knows well the impact such tournaments have in raising the side's profile at home and abroad.

"We're laser-focused on 50-over cricket right now for that reason," said Wilson of World Cup qualification.

"I've been lucky enough to be part of two and they are amazing experiences."

Stirling returns for Wilson's first Ireland ODIs

Security plans in place for any Afghanistan protests

Ireland are 12th in the ODI rankings and, as part of a keenly debated new format, will take part in a 10-team qualifier next year for just one guaranteed berth at the 2027 World Cup.

Another three teams will advance to a so-called Super Series directly preceding the tournament to decide the final spot in the 12-team field.

Despite the precarious path to even make it back to a World Cup, Wilson does not want his players to limit their ambition to just taking part.

"Irish cricket is really in its infancy in many ways and there's been a lot of firsts within the last 20 years," he said.

"We've had Ed Joyce as the first player to play for England, we've had the first World Cup in 2007, we've had the first Test win, why can't we go on and do something huge at a World Cup? If you'd said 30 or 40 years ago where the Irish rugby team would be now, you'd have got laughed at.

"Whether it's in our lifetime or not, one day we will do something amazing. A challenge I've put to this group is to create their own firsts. I think if we just stay focused, there's something big very close."

Should Ireland meet Wilson's ambitions, it will be in spite of a lack of 50-over cricket. In the three years since the 2023 edition of the World Cup, they have scheduled just 15 ODIs with three of those lost to the weather.

The series against Afghanistan - which Cricket Ireland CEO Sarah Keane has said comes with "moral discomfort" given the treatment of women in the Asian country - will be Ireland's first in the format since a 1-1 draw with West Indies in May 2025.

"It is a challenge of course, but it is what it is," said Wilson.

"We know it's a barrier but there's not any point in talking about it, we can't change it. We have played other cricket within that period.

"Would I have wanted more? Of course, I'd have wanted loads, but that's not to be. We've got what we've got and we get on with it and attempt to beat Afghanistan in this series."

Ireland at least come in with recent white-ball form after June's historic T20 series win over India.

The 2-0 victory at Stormont, Ireland's first wins over the T20 world champions in any format, made global headlines but Wilson is keen to draw a line under the feat.

"More than anything those results probably made people stand up and think and it's something we can try and work off the back of as a wider organisation," he said.

"In terms of the team, we mustn't get carried away with two results. You wouldn't change them for the world, they were phenomenal, but they're in the past now. We must start again against Afghanistan."

Bowler Jai Moondra, the breakout star of the India series, will make his 50-over debut against Afghanistan, while Paul Stirling, who retains the ODI captaincy despite relinquishing the T20 role, seamer Mark Adair and all-rounder Curtis Campher all return to the panel.

Against a side who have travelled with the likes of Rashid Kahn and Ibrahim Zadran in their touring squad, Ireland will however be without Josh Little, Craig Young, Barry McCarthy, Matt Hollard and Jordan Neil through injury.

The wins over India were the final games under previous head coach Heinrich Malan who was replaced by his former assistant Wilson less than 24 hours after the series concluded in what Cricket Ireland called a "planned transition".

While Wilson said the role is one he had his "eye on" since retiring in 2020, he acknowledges it will come with a different set of responsibilities to those he had under Malan.

"Obviously the relationships will have to change slightly because you become the person responsible for picking players and not picking players," he said.

"By default, some players aren't going to be happy and previously those players maybe would have turned to you.

"That's a different dynamic, but I base my whole coaching philosophy around communication and I think if you can remain pretty steady with that, while difficult conversations are hard, at least if you're honest, players know what to expect from you."

fullText:
United States international Bodugum Akhilesh Reddy has been banned from all forms of cricket for eight years after being found guilty of match-fixing.

An International Cricket Council (ICC) Anti-Corruption Tribunal found Reddy breached three counts of the sport's anti-corruption code during the Abu Dhabi T10 League in the United Arab Emirates last year.

The 26-year-old was part of the Aspin Stallions side that also featured former India off-spinner Harbhajan Singh and England's Sam Billings and which reached the Abu Dhabi T10 final in 2025.

The spinner made his USA debut against Cayman Islands in April 2025 and has played four T20s for the country.

The ICC said the tribunal found Reddy guilty of "attempting to fix, contrive or otherwise influence improperly, or being party to an agreement or effort to fix or contrive in any way or otherwise influence improperly, the result, progress, conduct or other aspect of matches in the ADT10 2025".

He was also found guilty of encouraging another participant to engage in match-fixing and obstructing the investigation "through deletion of data and messages from a mobile device".

The ban has been backdated to 21 November 2025 when Reddy was provisionally suspended after making two appearances in the T10 League.

title: Vinicius’ Real Madrid current contract details as renewal talks deadlocked due to image rights
description: Vinicius Jr.’s contract situation remains one of Real Madrid’s biggest unresolved issues, with negotiations stretching back to the aftermath of the 2025 Club World Cup, shortly after Xabi Alonso t...
fullText:
Vinicius Jr.’s contract situation remains one of Real Madrid’s biggest unresolved issues, with negotiations stretching back to the aftermath of the 2025 Club World Cup, shortly after Xabi Alonso took charge.

Indeed, as reported by AS, it was during that period that the player’s representatives held their last face-to-face meeting with the club, when an agreement appeared close before talks unexpectedly stalled.

Negotiations are now set to resume from that point.

During that meeting at Valdebebas, Vinicius reportedly made a significant concession on his original salary demands, which had initially been close to €30 million net per season.

Real Madrid also improved their offer, bringing both sides much closer together. Despite the progress, the renewal was never finalized.

Neither party was willing to make the final compromise, leaving an agreement that seemed imminent unsigned.

Still no agreement over renewal. (Photo by Lars Baron/Getty Images)

Vinicius is now seeking a salary of around €20 million net per season, an increase of roughly €5 million over his current earnings.

His existing contract, signed in 2022 and officially announced in October 2023, runs until 2027 and is worth €75 million net over five seasons, averaging €15 million per year.

The agreement was structured progressively. He began on approximately €10 million net per season. His salary rose annually to reach around €18 million in the final year.

The 26-year-old Brazilian also received an additional €2 million per season after winning FIFA’s The Best award, a bonus that would also have been triggered by winning the Ballon d’Or.

While salary remains important, image rights have become one of the biggest sticking points in negotiations.

Kylian Mbappe controls almost 100% of his image rights, a structure that helps facilitate his overall financial package at Real Madrid.

Vinicius is now looking for a similar arrangement. As one of football’s biggest commercial stars, the Brazilian has endorsement deals with 18 international brands.

These include Nike, Apple, PlayStation, Pepsi, Gatorade, Boss, Visa, Marriott Bonvoy, Havaianas, UNESCO, Clear, Rexona, Omo, Vivo, Prada, Dubai Tourism, and Betnacional.

The winger is also believed to be interested in receiving a renewal bonus, similar in concept to the signing bonus Mbappe received when joining Real Madrid.

Vinicius’ current deal expires in 2027, meaning that from January he would be permitted to negotiate freely with clubs outside Spain if no renewal is agreed.

As such, Real Madrid are seeking a quick resolution, one way or the other.

The latest information from the Brazilian’s camp suggests his priority remains staying at Real Madrid by signing a new contract.

Having returned to Valdebebas today after his vacation, Vinicius is expected to hold a decisive meeting with Jose Mourinho and Real Madrid’s senior leadership in the coming hours to discuss his future.

title: Chevron CEO warns Iran conflict has created 'very real' threat to global oil supplies as gas prices climb
description: Chevron CEO Mike Wirth warns of "very real" risks to oil supply as the Strait of Hormuz, Red Sea and Black Sea face growing threats amid Iran conflict.
fullText:
Chevron CEO Mike Wirth warned of "very real" dangers for the global oil industry as tensions escalate in Iran and Houthi attacks on Saudi oil facilities fuel concerns over a potential new shipping crisis.

His comments come as oil prices climb following President Donald Trump's pause on U.S. strikes against Iran and as Saudi Arabia reportedly builds an international coalition to protect vital shipping routes.

"We now see, not only the Strait of Hormuz, but the Red Sea and the Black Sea have risks and uncertainties. So, some of the challenges have expanded, and the risks to supply are very real," Wirth said during an appearance on "Sunday Morning Futures."

Trump Warns Iran Fighting Isn't Over As He Vows Us Will 'Win' As Talks Fade

While oil demand remains strong around the world, Wirth said energy markets are "fragile and uncertain" as the U.S. conflict with Iran festers into a sixth month and as global inventories continue to decline.

"The world energy system has been stressed and the need for supplies to markets and customers has never been higher," the Chevron CEO said.

The Strait of Hormuz, one of the world's most vital trade routes, is one of the most contentious aspects of the United States conflict with Iran. Traffic has sunk to only a handful of vessels passing through the waterway each day.

Recent Houthi attacks on another vital Middle East shipping route, the Red Sea, have raised fresh concerns about the reliability of that corridor.

Steve Forbes Urges Trump To Keep The Strait Of Hormuz Open At All Costs

"I think the unfortunate thing is that energy assets have been targeted in this conflict. And what that means is it degrades the capacity of the energy system to meet global demand," Wirth said. "And how quickly that comes back will be one of the things that determines when markets actually get back to some sort of a new equilibrium."

"We've seen supply constrained, we've seen damage to infrastructure. And we have new risks that I think will be priced into the market on shipping."

U.S. crude oil is trading at roughly $84 per barrel, while the national average price for a gallon of gasoline stands at $4.09 – nearly $1 higher than the $3.15 average one year ago, according to AAA.

Despite the growing geopolitical uncertainty, Chevron's production is up 20% year-on-year, with a 5% increase from Q1 to Q2 of 2026. The oil giant also set a record for producing more than 2 million barrels of oil equivalent in one day, an all-time high for the U.S., Wirth said.

title: UFC or PFL? Nurmagomedov to decide future 'very soon'
description: PFL lightweight world champion Usman Nurmagomedov will decide on his future "very soon" after becoming a free agent, according to his cousin and coach Khabib Nurmagomedov.
fullText:
PFL lightweight world champion Usman Nurmagomedov will decide on his future "very soon" after becoming a free agent, according to his cousin and coach Khabib Nurmagomedov.

Russia's Nurmagomedov knocked out American Archie Colgan in New York last week to retain his title in the final fight on his contract with the PFL.

The 28-year-old, who is undefeated with 22 victories, is widely-considered one of the biggest talents outside the UFC and has long been touted to eventually sign with the promotion.

But the end of his contract comes amid an exciting new chapter for the PFL after the organisation merged with Most Valuable Promotions (MVP) last week.

In a statement on Instagram, Khabib praised Nurmagomedov and compared him to team-mate and UFC welterweight champion Islam Makhachev, before revealing negotiations around his next move will take place "over the next month".

"Usman has shown and proven over the last couple of years that he is the best lightweight outside the UFC. Not with words, but with his performances," said Khabib.

"When I said in 2020 that Islam was the best at that time, there were many people who disagreed. Believe me guys, there are levels to this game.

"You will see for yourselves what happens next. There will be negotiations over the next month, and very soon you will find out for yourselves which league he will continue competing in."

Nurmagomedov's first-round knockout of Colgan was the second defence of his PFL belt and sixth in total after the Bellator title was rebranded in 2025.

After the bout, Nurmagomedov asked MVP co-owner Jake Paul for a "bonus", to which the American replied, "next fight if you get a knockout, I'll buy you a car".

Nurmagomedov raised questions about his future in the organisation by responding, "brother let's talk about today - we don't know what's going to happen tomorrow".

Following the UFC's event in Belgrade on Saturday, the promotion's president Dana White replied "sure" while sporting a wry smile when he was asked about the prospect of signing Nurmagomedov.

Paul has been a frequent critic of White and UFC fighter pay, and Nurmagomedov made reference to that in the closing words of his post-fight interview.

"MVP, they always trash talk about Dana saying he doesn't pay - now we're gonna see how they're gonna pay," said Nurmagomedov.

Fans have long wondered how Nurmagomedov would fare in the UFC with his career following a similar trajectory to cousin and coach, Khabib.

Former UFC lightweight champion Khabib retired undefeated in 2020 having won all 29 professional fights and cementing his legacy as one of the sport's greatest-ever fighters.

Khabib's game was built on relentless pressure and wrestling and although Nurmagomedov is fine grappler, he differs from his legendary cousin by controlling fights with an array of eye-catching kicks.

Like Khabib, Nurmagomedov is undefeated, but apart from two gruelling bouts with Paul Hughes in 2025, he has rarely been tested to his limit in the PFL.

Signing with the UFC would open doors to a number of mouth-watering fights, and although the move would be beneficial for his brand and name, financially the prospect is not as clear.

The UFC gives about 20% of revenue to fighter pay - a policy which has been criticised by fighters - while it remains to be seen what pay structure the PFL and MVP's merger will implement.

Whichever promotion pays Nurmagomedov the most may influence his decision, with the Russian admitting he values money over legacy in interviews following his win over Colgan.

title: Emma Finucane: Can cycling's new star be beaten?
description: Experts explain what sets apart this "generational talent" who is already an Olympic, world and commonwealth champion at just 23.
fullText:
Emma Finucane left Glasgow with four Commonwealth gold medals. She had become the conversation inside the Sir Chris Hoy Velodrome.

Not simply because she kept winning but because of the way she was winning.

A dominant week in Glasgow does not automatically make someone the best rider on the planet.

The world's best track cyclists are spread well beyond the Commonwealth.

As the week unfolded, conversations drifted away from the medal table.

And where this "generational talent" might be by the time the Los Angeles Olympics arrive in 2028.

BBC Sport spoke to the people who worked closest with Finucane throughout the Games to understand why those inside the velodrome believed they had witnessed far more than just an outstanding medal haul.

Those people do not first talk about Finucane's power or speed, but rather her methodical preparation.

"She's a dream to coach. It's the fact that she gets everything right off the bike in the lead-up to it is why she's able to perform on the track," said Team Wales sprint coach Rachel Draper.

Rob Partridge, a former professional cyclist who was part of Team Wales' coaching staff in Glasgow, describes an athlete who takes complete ownership of every detail.

"Everything she does is elite. She'll map everything out, be clear and concise and be first to send it," Partridge explains.

"Everything is super crisp and planned out."

Finucane's record-breaking day to remember

'I can't believe I'm living this life' - Finucane

'A huge success' - Wales win 31 medals at Glasgow Games

Preparation explained part of the conversation. Watching her ride explained the rest.

Again and again, people used the same word. Smooth.

"She's got a beautiful style. You could put a teacup on her back and it would not spill," said two-time Commonwealth champion Katherine Bates.

"She's got an exceptionally strong core. She does not move at all on the bike, even when putting out maximum power."

Paralympic gold medalist and Finucane's former Great Britain team-mate, Jenny Holl, believes that style is difficult to teach.

"Emma looks like she's one with the bike," she reveres.

"She's so smooth, so dialed. She never looks like she's fighting with it and, for me, that's the biggest difference. That fluidity seems to give her that extra gear."

Finucane's positioning has taken years of refining and discipline.

"She's so low but that's really hard work. She's trained herself to be in that position," explained Partridge.

"The work she's put in, the focus on the position and the discipline on her line, all these things add up to making her what she is."

Perhaps the best example came in the women's 1km time trial.

While most of the field opted for specialist time-trial handlebars, Finucane chose conventional drop handlebars.

Finucane left Paris an Olympic champion after winning gold in the team sprint.

But Holl believes those 2024 Games left her wanting more.

"The bronze medals in the [individual] sprint and keirin in Paris, where she wanted gold, have given Emma that extra boost of motivation," she said.

"She was a brilliant athlete in Paris, but now we really are seeing something special."

Another quality kept surfacing throughout the week - composure.

Bates says Finucane rarely betrays what she is feeling.

"She's so determined, but she's also so calm. Even under pressure, you just never see anything on her face but composure," she said.

"She barely even cracks a smile until it's over. That's part of how she prepares for an event.

"It's a big build-up. She maintains that and when it's over, she releases the pressure valve and moves on to the next one."

For Draper, these Games in the red lycra of Wales mattered deeply to Finucane.

"Emma put a lot of pressure on herself to perform at these Games," she said.

"She's already world champion, Olympic champion, but for Emma, this has meant everything.

"Seeing that emotion for her on the podium has just been really special for us as a team."

When Bates reflects on the greatest female sprinters she has watched, her thoughts turn to Anna Meares, Victoria Pendleton and Kristina Vogel.

"Emma Finucane is like a combination of them all rolled up into one neat package," explained the former world points race champion.

"Some have incredible acceleration, others are very good at the back end of a long race.

"There are others whose skills are just superior. She's got excellent skills, acceleration and really good staying power, so it makes her a triple threat.

"She's young that she hasn't gone to four Olympic Games yet, or 15 World Championships that some of the others have.

"But I'm fairly confident in a decade's time we'll be looking back at her career, just wondrous of what she's been able to achieve."

Then comes the line that echoed around the Sir Chris Hoy Velodrome.

"A lot of the countries are looking at her and thinking, 'Is it even worth trying to beat her? Or are we going there for a silver medal?'," admitted Australian Bates.

"That's a big statement two years out [from the Olympics] but that's the kind of talent we're looking at."

Four gold medals made Finucane the most successful cyclist of the Games and her nation's most decorated female Commonwealth Games athlete.

For those who know the sport best, they may also have been a glimpse of what comes next.

fullText:
Newcastle United’s search for a new first-choice goalkeeper is finally over after months of speculation surrounding the position and a lengthy list of reported targets throughout the summer.

The Magpies officially announced the signing of Czech Republic international Lukas Hornicek from Braga on Monday, with the 24-year-old arriving on a five-year contract after Newcastle activated his €30 million (£25.7 million) release clause.

The Athletic reported the deal’s figures, revealing it would be worth the full value of the goalkeeper’s release clause, which Newcastle activated over the weekend.

Hornicek becomes Newcastle’s fifth first-team signing of the summer following the arrivals of Ewen Jaouen, Bazoumana Toure, Sean Steur and Aladji Bamba. The goalie has already joined the team at Newcastle’s preseason training camp in Spain, with new manager Matthias Jaissle in town but still not officially hired, as no word from the club has emerged since Eddie Howe’s exit.

Speaking after completing the move, Hornicek described the transfer as a major opportunity.

“The last few days have been an emotional rollercoaster from when I first heard about the move and now I’m so happy to be here,” Hornicek said. “It’s a brilliant opportunity in a new league, which I’m very excited about.”

The goalkeeper also highlighted Newcastle’s supporters as one of the attractions behind the move.

“I know Newcastle is a huge football city, with 52,000 fans at St. James’ Park creating an incredible atmosphere and pushing the team every game,” Hornicek said. “I can’t wait to play in front of them.”

Sporting director Ross Wilson believes the club has secured one of Europe’s brightest young goalkeepers.

“His progress in recent years has been remarkable and he has firmly established himself as one of Europe’s top young goalkeepers,” Wilson said. “We knew there would be no shortage of clubs interested in acquiring Lukáš this summer after everything he achieved last season, but it quickly became evident how keen he was to be a part of what we are building here.”

Hornicek played a key role in Braga’s run to the Europa League semifinals last season, helping the Portuguese side finish fourth in Portugal’s Primeira Liga while keeping 12 clean sheets and conceding just 33 league goals. He also earned his first senior Czech Republic cap earlier this year before being included in the nation’s World Cup squad.

title: When the Future Doesn't Need Us
description: What does the world look like when AI outcompetes humans?
fullText:
Today, the world is made of people. This gives people a tiny measure of
leverage: factory workers can sabotage the machines and halt production, truck
drivers can strike and halt the entire economy, the police can stand back and
let a protest topple the government, the military can
mutiny. This sets a limit to how much the powerful can abuse the
powerless: no matter how powerful someone is, how much money they have, how many
divisions they command, they are still embedded in a society. They need other
people to survive, and to maintain their quality of life. And those people can,
essentially, veto the political order by withdrawing their contribution to it.

AI changes this. If AI works the factories, drives the trucks, does most of the
white collar work, fights the wars, then humans become materially powerless. We
lose one type of leverage against power. We become disempowered. When
people talk about AI taking jobs, the main problems they worry about are poverty
and meaning, but I think more people should be worried about disempowerment.

But what if there is no mass unemployment? After all, we’ve spent two hundred
years automating one job after another, and every advanced economy is de facto
at full employment. We keep discovering new, higher-level, better-paying jobs to
do. So maybe the AIs take today’s jobs, and humans move one level up, to work
newer jobs. Alex Imas, in What will be scarce?, describes
what this looks like:

As commodity production gets automated, income and employment flow toward the
sectors with high income elasticity: what I am calling the relational sector,
including the arts but also care, education, hospitality, therapy, personal
services, craftsmanship, and community, where the human element is part of the
value.

If the model is right, the durable jobs of the future won’t be about
monitoring AI systems or prompt engineering. Those are transitional roles in
the automated sector. The durable jobs will be in the relational sector, where
the human element is the product itself.

Some already exist and are growing: nurses, therapists, teachers, boutique
fitness instructors, personal chefs, bespoke tailors, craft brewers, live
performers, spiritual guides, childcare workers, and many varieties of
hospitality and care work. Others are emerging: experience designers, human-AI
collaboration artists, provenance certifiers, community curators. Many haven’t
been invented yet, just as six out of ten jobs people hold today didn’t exist
in 1940.

So, in this world, we get mass job displacement, but not mass unemployment. I
argue that in this world, we’d still be disempowered.

If all the podcasters in the world go on strike, what happens? Nothing. Same for
the boutique fitness instructors, personal chefs, craft brewers, etc. The
problem with the “relational economy” is that while these jobs are generally
nicer than working in manufacturing, and might pay better, they put you further
away from material reality. A worker at an assembly line can sabotage the
machines; whereas an executive sitting in an office on the other side of the
country, what material power do they have? It’s not like the factories are all
rigged to blow, as a “pull lever in case of nationalization” contingency. I
doubt even Elon would do that.

In a sense it’s the dual version of being a medieval peasant. Peasants had a lot
of material leverage—they grew all the food—but were illiterate and poor and
dispersed, so they could not coordinate to exploit that leverage. People in
industrial societies are literate, relatively wealthy, and concentrated in urban
centers: they have material leverage and the ability to exploit it. People in
post-AI societies will be in constant communication, they may be literate and
educated, but they will have no material power whatever. And so they will have
no way to physically withdraw the consent of the governed.

In the post-AGI world, people have no way to withdraw the consent of the
governed. They can’t resist economically, because they are economically
unnecessary: if they still have jobs, they won’t be materially vital jobs. Even
if they could resist, they can’t coordinate their resistance, because AGI will
make mass surveillance (the physical and legal infrastructure for which already
exists) a thousandfold more effective, since with intelligence too cheap to
meter, you can have a superhumanly-capable intelligence analyst assigned to each
human. And if the AIs fight the wars, they can also fight the civil wars. So
people can’t resist violently either, because drones controlled by powerful AGI
almost certainly have a better K/D ratio than humans with rifles (and are
cheaper to build).

Who has power in this world? The few humans who give orders to the powerful AIs
that control the killing machines. And probably not for long, since sooner or
later those humans will be usurped by their AIs.

It might be the case that liberal democracies can remain liberal and democratic
despite not needing their voters. But that sounds like a fragile arrangement, in
which liberal democracy is a spandrel, which exists more because of
inertia than because it’s necessary.

If we get powerful AGI, but none of this happens: why didn’t it happen? Some
possibilities, sorted by decreasing likelihood:

If you’re already convinced, you can stop reading. But, see, after writing the
first version of this post, I wasn’t convinced. Humans and Claudes made a number
of counterarguments that I felt were important. Am I fooling myself? So I sat
down to think some more. What does it mean for “people” to be “empowered”? What
does “disempowerment” mean? Does it mean anything rigorous, or is it just an
emotional cue?

Let’s say a group of people is empowered if they have a say in the political
order of the state they live in. Voters in a democratic society are empowered,
at least in the aggregate, while serfs in the Russian Empire were disempowered.

Who is empowered, in general? Historically, in many places: people with weapons,
asabiyyah, and the ability to coordinate their actions. So, maybe we
can say that power equals violence plus coordination.

(What about priests and other such groups who have power despite not fighting or
working? Listen, we can’t be here all day. This isn’t meant to be a complete
theory of political science and I’ve already gone too deep with the LaTeX and
the logical notation.)

Now, voters in modern democracies have a say in the political order, though they
are not part of a military elite. Why? They have coordination (thanks to mass
literacy and modern communications) but they generally don’t threaten
paramilitary violence. What do they have that can substitute for violence? Maybe
it’s that people do all the work, and if they stop doing their jobs, the army
runs out of food, police don’t get paid, etc., and unlike medieval peasants,
modern people can coordinate. So maybe we can refine the formula to:

In other words, for a group to be empowered, they need:

What about the Soviet Union? They had high rates of literacy, and relatively
modern communication technology: why didn’t the people exploit their economic
leverage against the state to gain political rights? “Because the state would
kill them” is not a good enough explanation because it proves too much: under
that model, no country would liberalize and democratize. I think a reasonable
explanation is that the state’s repression was enough to effectively neuter
people’s ability to coordinate: every communication technology was surveilled
and censored.

Now, doesn’t this argument imply that, as a country’s employment moves towards
services, the country’s politics should become more authoritarian, while in
reality we observe the opposite? But whether a country’s economy is 5% or 95%
services, the material side of the economy is equally vital. So “aggregate
empowerment” remains as employment becomes more and more abstract. Consider
France, where the economy is ~80% services, but the last 20% can still paralyze
the country through strikes. In a sense every knowledge worker is free-riding on
the ability of truck drivers and dock workers to shut down the economy. I don’t
greatly like this counter-counterargument, though, because it’s hard to falsify:
it implies that countries might remain liberal democracies until AGI replaces
all humans in material work, at which point the state can go “that’s what we
wanted you to think!” and go full authoritarian.

fullText:
Online multiplayer changed the trajectory of games, but the cost of keeping servers running means every virtual world is doomed to die – sooner or later

Nevan Hagarty had an idea. If he and other Halo 3 players stayed online the night of 13 January 2022, they could delay the impending server shutdown. Players knew this was coming: it had happened to Halo 2 when its Xbox Live servers were turned off in 2010, and a group managed to stay logged into the multiplayer servers for weeks.

And so, players gathered online before the server shutdown to pay homage and to mourn the game they loved so dearly. And, maybe, to keep it online for a little longer. “I must have played ’til about 4am the night of the shutdown, trading stories with so many players about their love of the game and their experiences over the last 15 years,” says Hagarty, 22. “It was a really wholesome experience I won’t forget.”

A sense of mourning went both spoken and unspoken. Thirty-year-old fan Jimi hadn’t played Halo 3 in a while but logged on to the game on shutdown day to experience the original servers just once more, later posting a video on Reddit.

“My team was losing really bad,” he says, “I saw a few of the other team’s people standing in the middle, and our guy standing in the middle, and everybody’s just looking at each other. I shot up once in the air, and then everybody just starts going crazy.” Someone threw a shield down, others threw grenades in the air and launched rockets. It looked almost like fireworks. “There were no people on the voice chat. There wasn’t any mutual agreement on this. Everybody just felt it and knew.”

When online multiplayer came to video games in the late 90s, it meant that players from across the globe could interact with people they’d never otherwise meet. This changed the trajectory of video games, bringing people together in ways that games hadn’t before – to play, and to mourn, when their virtual worlds are doomed to die.

Games go offline all the time, and people have got used to saying goodbye to their favourites. The increasing popularity of online-only live service games means more reliance on servers to host these experiences. And those servers cost money to run and maintain; in the case of recent flop Highguard, developer Wildlight Entertainment couldn’t afford to keep the game online for more than a few months. Over twenty games have shut off their servers already in 2026.

“People really hold on to the idea of place,” says UX and games researcher Evan Conaway, who holds a PhD in anthropology. “That we create community online at all is really remarkable. When you find it and you have it and it’s real, you have an emotional connection to it. Wanting to hold on to it is only human.”

Conaway says this happens a lot in the real world, when the corner bar shutters, or a local skatepark is torn down. His research delved into the ways people commemorate online spaces, with a focus on the massively multiplayer online role-playing game World of Warcraft (WoW). People play together on separate servers – or instances – which all run contained copies of WoW, and each server has its own culture created by the community. When the game changes, the culture can change, too. WoW has persisted for decades, and the game is no longer the same as it was when it was released – it’s hardly the same game it was just a few years ago.

Though people still have access to WoW, they are often “gradually mourning”, says Conaway. They know that this version of the game is ephemeral. It won’t stay the same – it can’t, by design. In exchange for new content, players must accept that the spaces they inhabit online will find new forms. “The quests are different, the way things are worded is different,” he says. “The way I felt while playing it, and wandering around by myself or exploring the world, all of that is part of this meaning-making for people – just the raw experience of it.”

Part of Conaway’s research centred on a group of people who wanted to literally hold on to those memories and meanings. When Blizzard Entertainment was changing its servers in 2011, it auctioned off the old server blades with autographed placards displaying which server they held. It was important for some players, he says, to have a physical representation of that moment in time. He points to one server in particular, Proudmoore, which was an unofficial queer server: “For a gay person or queer person who was playing World of Warcraft at that time on that server, it does feel a little bit like a skatepark brick, like they can take home a piece of a thing.”

When World of Warcraft players in China were faced with server shutdowns in 2023, they were at the mercy of both Blizzard Entertainment and its Chinese partner NetEase. Games in China must be published with a local company, so when Blizzard Entertainment and NetEase had a dispute, it hit the players. Millions lost not just the server but the whole game, and there was no date set for its return. It could have been months, years. Maybe never.

Naturally, players wanted to gather in their servers on the day of the shutdown, 24 January 2023, to pay their respects. To do so, people started preparing – and logging in – days in advance, according to City University of Hong Kong PhD student and games researcher HongLan Xu, who joined them to document the last days.

“I encountered hundreds of players, but there are millions,” says Xu. “Everybody thought it could be at least several years. They don’t know when the server will be back. It’s profound. It’s real. The shutdown is very real for them, so they gathered in the game to say farewell to their avatars, like it’s the last time.”

Chinese players’ grief was mixed with anger, too, says Xu. Many in the Chinese market felt disrespected, as if Blizzard Entertainment didn’t care about them: “From a Chinese player’s perspective, the main takeaway is sometimes the capitalism of the western gaming companies [leads to] distrust.”

WoW opened back up to Chinese players in August 2024. Returning players were glad to have it back, of course, but there was an unease underneath that excitement. This could happen again; they knew what it felt like to lose it all. “Virtual life attachment and this sense of loss is deep, profound,” says Xu. “It can be completely vulnerable and very uncertain.”

Losing your forever-game is a uniquely sad experience. Players make a very real investment into these spaces – time, money, friendships, stories, characters, creativity. As one player put it, “What gets me is that people poured themselves into these games. Not just cash, but actual time, actual friendships built inside them, characters they spent months on. And then one day a studio decides the numbers don’t work any more and everything just disappears.”

title: Blue Jays reportedly trade Kevin Gausman to Cubs, signaling sell-off months after World Series appearance
description: The deal in part signals a Blue Jays selloff at the MLB trade deadline, months after they took the Dodgers to extra innings in Game 7 of the World Series.
fullText:
The Toronto Blue Jays have traded starting pitcher Kevin Gausman to the Chicago Cubs, signaling a sell-off at the MLB trade deadline months after they took the Dodgers to extra innings in Game 7 of the World Series.

The Athletic's Ken Rosenthal and Mitch Bannon reported the trade on Sunday, hours before Monday's 6 p.m. ET trade deadline. In return, according to the report, the Blue Jays will receive outfielder Brett Bateman and infielder Ty Southisene, both prospects.

The move in part cements a season of disappointment for the Blue Jays, who started 2026 with hopes of competing for the AL East title and returning to the postseason. Instead, they've entered the stretch run in last place in the division at 52-60 with long-shot hopes of competing for a wild-card spot.

Whether the Blue Jays would be sellers at the deadline or hold steady for a shot at the postseason was unclear before the All-Star break. But they lost five of their first six games coming out of the break, including three to the AL East-leading Tampa Bay Rays.

Gausman is playing on the final season of a five-year, $110 million contract. He was a prime candidate for a deadline deal to a contending team seeking a contributor with an expiring contract.

A two-time All-Star, Gausman isn't at his peak form at 35 years old. But he's been a reliable starter for much of his career, including this season as one of MLB's leaders in starts and innings pitched.

Gausman provides the Cubs with a mid-rotation option days after they designated veteran Jameson Taillon for assignment.

Taillon, 34, was in the midst of a career-worst season with a 5.92 ERA and 25 home runs allowed. Chicago traded Taillon to Toronto in a separate deal earlier Sunday for cash considerations or a player to be named later.

Taillon pitched 76 innings for the Cubs this season, and his departure left Chicago with a hole in their rotation. Gausman, who's made 14 postseason appearances, slots in for what the Cubs hope is an upgrade for the stretch run and a likely playoff appearance.

The Cubs leave a 2-1 loss to the Yankees on Sunday at 63-49, in control of first place in the NL wild-card standings with a four-game cushion over second. They're 6.5 game behind the Brewers for first place in the NL Central.

Per MLB Pipeline, Southisene ranked as Chicago's No. 13 prospect, and Bateman rated at No. 21. Neither are in MLB Pipeline's top 100 overall prospects. They're both now building blocks for Toronto's future.

title: Pegula leads Eala as storms push Washington Open finals to Monday
description: World number three Jessica Pegula and rising star Alexandra Eala must wait until Monday to decide a Washington Open champion after thunderstorms postponed the completion of Sunday's WTA final.Eala ousted former world number one Naomi Osaka, second seed Elina Svitolina and defending champion Leylah Fernandez to reach the final.
fullText:
World number three Jessica Pegula and rising star Alexandra Eala must wait until Monday to decide a Washington Open champion after thunderstorms postponed the completion of Sunday's WTA final.

After waiting through a three-hour thunderstorm delay to start, Pegula won the first set 6-4 and Eala led 2-1 in the second set of the championship match when rain returned.

More than five hours passed with conditions remaining unplayable before organizers called off the resumption of play until Monday.

Also postponed was the entire men's final at the WTA and ATP 500-level hardcourt tournament, with 10th-ranked American Taylor Fritz set to face 19-year-old Spaniard Rafael Jodar.

The women's final will resume Monday at noon local time (1600 GMT) with the men's final not before 1 p.m. in Washington.

Pegula, who won her first WTA title in 2019 at Washington, seeks her 12th tour trophy and third of the year after Dubai and Charleston.

The 32-year-old American top seed defeated Eala in a 2025 Miami semi-final in their only prior meeting.

Philippines star Eala, cheered all week by a host of supporters, seeks her first WTA title in her second career final, having lost last year at Eastbourne.

The 21-year-old left-hander is set to jump to a career-best 24th in the world rankings.

Eala ousted former world number one Naomi Osaka, second seed Elina Svitolina and defending champion Leylah Fernandez to reach the final.

Pegula broke Eala in the fifth game, blasting a forehand service return winner, only for Eala to break back at love to 3-3 on a blistering backhand service return winner.

Pegula saved two break points in holding to 4-4, broke again when Eala sent a forehand long in the ninth game and held at love to capture the first set in 40 minutes when Eala hit a backhand beyond the baseline.

Players were on serve and in a changeover when the rain returned.

In 53 minutes before the stoppage, Pegula hit 14 winners to only four by Eala while both had 20 unforced errors.

In the men's final, Fritz seeks an 11th career ATP title and his first since last year at Eastbourne.

Jodar, assured of reaching a career-high 15th in next week's rankings, seeks his second ATP crown after winning at Morocco in April.

title: Sri Lanka star recalls biggest Gautam Gambhir 'regret' from India's 2011 World Cup final, match-winning six by MS Dhoni
description: 15 years from that fateful day when India won the 2011 World Cup, one former Sri Lankan star remembers Dhoni's match-winning six and his regret for dropping Gautam Gambhir's catch.
fullText:
Sri Lanka star recalls biggest Gautam Gambhir 'regret' from India's 2011 World Cup final, match-winning six by MS Dhoni originally appeared on Cricket News. Add Cricket News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.

Former Sri Lanka pacer Nuwan Kulasekara still regrets dropping Gautam Gambhir in the 2011 World Cup final.

MS Dhoni's match-winning six off his bowling sealed India's title at the Wankhede.

Kulasekara later played under Dhoni at CSK and admired his calm nature.

Nuwan Kulasekara remains haunted by the defining moments of the 2011 World Cup final, a match in which he was on the wrong end of one of cricket's most iconic images. The former Sri Lanka pacer, now bowling coach of Lanka Premier League franchise Colombo Kaps, revisited the painful memories in a candid interview.

Speaking exclusively to RevSportz at the team hotel in Kandy, Kulasekara reflected on a night that ended in heartbreak for Sri Lanka. India chased down 275 at the Wankhede Stadium on April 2, 2011, with Gautam Gambhir's 97 laying the platform before Dhoni finished the job in emphatic fashion.

For Kulasekara, the defeat still stings, not least because of a costly moment in the field involving the man who would top-score for India. He was refreshingly honest about the part he played in a result that went the hosts' way.

MORE: Bhuvneshwar Kumar breaks silence on India comeback after R Ashwin backs him for World Cup

Kulasekara pinpointed a dropped chance as a moment he cannot forget. He said:

"Yes, at one stage we definitely believed we could win. I dropped an important catch off Gambhir, and naturally there is regret."

"But these moments happen in big matches. Ben Stokes experienced something similar in the 2016 T20 World Cup final before going on to play a match-winning role in England's 2019 World Cup triumph."

But Kulasekara hasn't let these moments sour his memories. He believes such is the nature of the sport. He also reflected on the six that sealed India's win, which he hit off his own bowling. Kulasekara said, "In cricket, especially during the powerplay and the death overs, such things can happen to any bowler."

He continued, "I tried my best to dismiss him, but he still hit me for a six. The positive memory is that we came back and won the 2014 T20 World Cup in a similar fashion. That is how this beautiful game works." Ironically, that wasn't the end of the dance between Dhoni and Kulasekara. The next time the two met, it was in franchise cricket.

MORE: Delhi Premier League 2026: Fixtures, scores & where to watch

Kulasekara ended up joining Chennai Super Kings and played under the very man (Dhoni) who had denied Sri Lanka a 2011 ODI World Cup title. What struck him most was Dhoni's refusal to dwell on that final.

"I joined Chennai Super Kings immediately after the World Cup, but Dhoni never spoke about that final. That shows the kind of person he is."

"He is incredibly calm and always focused on the present. For him, the past is over. His only concern was winning the next game. That is something I really admired about him," Kulasekara said.

Turning to the present, Kulasekara backed his countrymen to compete in the upcoming Test series against India, which begins in Galle on August 15. He said, "Playing at home in a World Test Championship series gives us the chance to show how competitive we are in Test cricket. I believe we can compete with them, especially because we are playing at home."

MORE: Arshdeep Singh apologises to Ashwin after placing India legend last in bowler rankings

There is something quietly moving about Kulasekara's willingness to own his part in that final rather than bury it. Fifteen years on, he neither hides from the dropped catch nor the six, framing both as the inevitable cruelties of elite sport, a maturity that speaks well of the man.

His admiration for Dhoni adds a further layer to the tale. The captain who inflicted the deepest wound on Sri Lankan cricket became a figure Kulasekara came to respect at close quarters, a reminder that the game's fiercest rivalries often soften into mutual regard once the contest is done.

title: Chelsea sign notorious World Cup star from sister club Strasbourg
description: Barco, who was involved in a viral heated exchange with Jude Bellingham after the World Cup semi-final, has moved to Stamford Bridge on a seven-year deal
fullText:
Chelsea have signed Argentina international Valentin Barco from sister club Strasbourg on a seven-year deal.

The 22-year-old, who played seven times for Brighton including six Premier League appearances during the 2023-24 season, becomes the seventh arrival of new manager Xabi Alonso’s reign.

A versatile player who can be used in central midfield as well as his regular position of left-back, Barco was in the Argentina squad that finished as runners-up at the World Cup, winning his fifth cap in the 3-1 group-stage win over Jordan.

He moved to Strasbourg initially on loan from Brighton in 2024 but signed permanently a year later having helped the club to qualify for the Conference League.

In all he made 53 appearances for the Ligue 1 side.

He was involved in a heated exchange with England’s Jude Bellingham immediately after his side’s 2-1 World Cup semi-final win in Atlanta, with Bellingham appearing to clip Barco around the head. An unused substitute, the Argentinian had earlier run onto the pitch to celebrate after Enzo Fernandez had equalised.

He is expected to join up shortly with his new team-mates on their tour of Australia and Hong Kong.

It continues a busy summer in the transfer market for Chelsea as they look to remodel under Alonso.

On Saturday they confirmed the signing of veteran striker Danny Welbeck from Brighton, following the signings of Crystal Palace’s Maxence Lacroix and Morgan Rogers from Aston Villa.

Marco Palestra, Emmanuel Emegha and Geovany Quenda have also been signed.

title: Body of famed international climber Nirmal Purja and 3 more found after Pakistan avalanche
description: The remains of renowned British-Nepali climber Nirmal Purja and three other climbers have been found by a ground team on Broad Peak, one of the world’s highest mountains, where a 10-member internation...
fullText:
ISLAMABAD (AP) — The remains of renowned British-Nepali climber Nirmal Purja and three other climbers have been found by a ground team on Broad Peak, one of the world's highest mountains, where a 10-member international expedition was swept away by an avalanche, officials said Sunday.

The Alpine Club of Pakistan identified the recovered climbers as Purja, Wang Zhong, Nima Sherpa and Kili Pemba Sherpa. The club praised military and civilian rescuers and volunteers involved in the recovery effort.

On Friday, rescuers located four other bodies but were able to recover only three — Omani Nathira Ahmed, American Mallory Geis and Nepalese Bahadur Gurung — because harsh weather grounded search-and-rescue helicopters.

Military-backed rescue teams resumed the search Sunday for the two remaining climbers, while efforts continued to bring down the bodies of Purja and the three others found by the ground team, local officials said.

On Saturday, Purja's expedition company said the world had lost one of mountaineering's greats. The company described him as "a leader who inspired millions through his courage, humility and unwavering belief that human potential is far greater than we often imagine."

Alpine Club of Pakistan President Irfan Arshad Khan said the tragedy was "an immeasurable loss to the global mountaineering fraternity." He paid tribute to military and civilian rescuers and Sherpas who took part in the search mission.

The expedition was led by Purja, the Nepal-born former British Army soldier widely known as Nims Dai.

He climbed the world's 14 highest peaks in a record 189 days in 2019, an achievement featured in the Netflix documentary "14 Peaks: Nothing Is Impossible." His record was broken in 2023.

A statement from Geis' family said, "Mallory was a bright light who was loved deeply by her family and friends. She will be profoundly missed."

The expedition was expected to be the last one for Pakistani guide Sohail Sakhi, who worked with Moving Mountains, a Pakistan-based adventure travel company. Sakhi also was a geographer and high-altitude photographer who had climbed some of the world's major peaks, according to the company's website. His body remained missing on Sunday.

Accidents are common on climbing expeditions in northern Pakistan because of avalanches, falling ice and rock, extreme altitude and rapidly changing weather.

Riaz Khan reported from Peshawar, Pakistan.

title: Trump beats Wilson to clinch second Shanghai crown
description: World number one Judd Trump beats Kyren Wilson 11-6 to win the Shanghai Masters for the second time.
fullText:
World number one Judd Trump beat Kyren Wilson 11-6 to win the Shanghai Masters for the second time.

Trump, 36, led 7-3 after the final's opening session before taking four of the next seven frames to clinch the first big event of the 2026-27 season.

Wilson won the 2025 competition with an 11-9 victory over Ali Carter and moved into an early lead on Sunday. But Trump responded well and took a 4-2 advantage, helped by breaks of 73, 62 and a 67 clearance in the sixth frame to take it on the black having trailed 66-0.

World number seven Wilson pulled one back, but Trump, who also won the tournament in 2024, took three frames in a row to hold a four-frame advantage after the first session.

He stretched that to five by winning the first frame after the restart before Wilson made a break of 103, the first century of the final, to pull it back to 8-4.

Wilson won the next too, but Trump took the 14th frame on the black and the 15th on the pink to move one away from the title.

An excellent clearance of 134 from Wilson kept his hopes alive, but Trump sealed the 17th frame to lift the trophy once again.

"He's beaten me in the last few finals," Trump told the WST website. "It was nice to start the season in that kind of manner and get one over on him. This tournament is amazing. I love coming to Shanghai. It is the first tournament of the year and it is a bit unknown how you are going to play.

"The last time I won Shanghai I had a great season after that. You need to win tournaments like this to test yourself against the best. It was important to get off to a good start. I've done that, I just need to do the rest now."

The Shanghai Masters is a non-ranking event, but one of the most lucrative on the World Snooker Tour (WST), with Trump collecting £210,000 and 34-year-old Wilson £105,000.

The tournament featured 24 players - the top 16 in the world rankings, the next four Chinese players as well as four Chinese wildcards.

It was Trump's first main tournament since a disappointing performance at the World Championship in April when he lost 13-12 to Iranian qualifier Hossein Vafaei in the last 16.

But in China he beat Barry Hawkins, John Higgins and reigning world champion Wu Yize before his victory over Wilson.

The first main ranking tournament of the season begins on Saturday when the China Open returns to the calendar for the first time since 2019.

It will take place in Taiyuan from 8-16 August, replacing the Saudi Arabia Snooker Masters, which was cancelled after only two years of a 10-year deal.

Trump will begin his campaign next Sunday against Thailand's Noppon Saengkham before Wilson plays his first-round tie against Ireland's Aaron Hill the following day.

title: China's free Kimi K3 AI model shakes up global tech market
description: Governments can now deploy top-tier AI locally, bypassing costly U.S. cloud rentals.
fullText:
The best artificial intelligence technology any country can own is now available for free.

On July 27, China’s Moonshot AI put its most powerful chatbot on the internet for anyone to use. The AlibabaiAlibabaAlibaba, founded in 1999 by Chinese entrepreneur Jack Ma, is one of the most prominent global e-commerce companies that operates platforms like AliExpress, Taobao, and Tmall.-backed developer released the software behind its AI model Kimi K3, allowing any government, company, or individual to run it on their own computers without paying Beijing-based Moonshot. Users can also retrain the chatbot to fit their own language and laws.

Nations are spending billions of dollars to run sovereign systems or AI on their own soil so that citizen data stays within their borders and can’t be accessed by foreign companies or governments. Most countries own the machines but lease the computing power and software from U.S. companies such as Microsoft, Google, and Amazon, which count on the rent continuing for years. Kimi K3 offers those governments a way out.

An open, high-quality model like Kimi K3 does change the calculation for governments.” Mohammed Soliman, senior fellow, Middle East Institute

“An open, high-quality model like Kimi K3 does change the calculation for governments that have been investing heavily in hardware while paying for access to American models,” Mohammed Soliman, a senior fellow at Washington-based think tank Middle East Institute, told Rest of World. “If a competitive model becomes freely available, the return on those hardware investments increases because governments can reduce or eliminate ongoing licensing costs.”

Kimi K3 ranks third on Artificial Analysis’s index of the best AI systems, behind Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5 and OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol Max, both of which charge users. Every free model in the world, including China’s DeepSeek and Meta’s Llama, sits below Kimi K3.

Kimi K3 reads images as well as text, so it can work through scanned records, forms and photographs, and it can be reshaped to answer in Hindi, Arabic or Swahili, among other languages, as easily as in Chinese or English.

The chatbot has closed China’s gap with the best U.S. AI systems from months to weeks, according to a July report by researcher Ryan Fedasiuk of the American Enterprise Institute, a public-policy think tank.

“Chinese open-weight models are growing in popularity around the world as free and customizable alternatives to the closed U.S. frontier,” Vivek Chilukuri, program director for technology and national security at the Center for a New American Security, told Rest of World. “That’s true not only in more cost-sensitive emerging markets but in developer communities from Bangalore to San Francisco.”

The savings from free models like Kimi K3 can be largest in the countries that have already bought the hardware. Microsoft, Google, and Amazon have committed to building data centers and cloud services worth more than $30 billion across the Gulf, and more than $45 billion in India, among other regions.

India signed a deal with United Arab Emirates-backed G42 to deploy an AI supercomputer made of 64 U.S.-made systems on Indian soil, while continuing to pay U.S. companies for AI software. For India and every government in the same position, a model of Kimi K3’s rank is an option to run on machines inside their own borders.

Still, being free is no guarantee that governments will adopt it.

Free Chinese models have been available for more than a year, yet no government has built its national AI project on one, as countries also judge the manuals, the legal terms, how well the software handles their languages, and where it comes from.

The Sovereign AI Index, which follows 139 state-backed AI projects across 56 countries and regions, found that where governments disclose the software underneath their AI, four in 10 chose Meta’s free U.S. model Llama, and not one chose DeepSeek or Moonshot’s earlier chatbots, even though those were free and highly rated.

Whether Kimi K3 breaks that pattern will likely depend partly on the support Moonshot provides and partly on government wariness about adopting Chinese models due to concerns of trust and surveillance, Pablo Chavez, an adjunct senior fellow at CNAS, which publishes the index, told Rest of World.

“That tells me benchmark position alone doesn’t change what sovereign builders do,” Chavez said. “Instead, governments appear to choose base models the way they choose other infrastructure — documentation, licensing, language coverage, capability, and so forth.”

Countries should encourage open source, Chinese President Xi Jinping told the World AI Conference in Shanghai on July 17, pledging AI cooperation centers with the Arab League, the African Union and ASEAN. Alibaba has since announced Qwen 3.8 with a promise to give it away, while Nvidia, Google and OpenAI have all released free models this year.

While software like Kimi K3 may cost nothing, the machines that run it come at a price. A chatbot of Kimi K3’s size runs only on the most advanced chips, and the U.S. decides which countries can buy those chips. The Commerce Department went further last year and considered cutting off Chinese AI labs from U.S. technology altogether.

“U.S. export controls continue to confer enormous leverage on Washington, because the world desperately wants cutting-edge AI chips, which you need regardless of whether you’re running a U.S. or Chinese model,” Chilukuri said.

China has yet to fill that gap, as its chipmakers are unable to produce their most advanced processors in quantities large enough to export, Chilukuri said. A country that downloads Kimi K3 gets the software and nothing else, while the chips it runs on, the data centers that house it, and whatever model comes after it remain in other hands, Chavez said.

“A government can hold a model’s weights and still depend on others for chips, data centers, and future models,” Chavez said. “Open weights address the risk of losing access, but they don’t remove the dependencies upstream.”

title: Bhuvneshwar Kumar breaks silence on India comeback after R Ashwin backs him for 2027 ODI World Cup
description: After a stellar IPL season in 2025 and 2026 with RCB, veteran pacer Bhuvneshwar Kumar has broken the silence on his Team India comeback after support from R Ashwin.
fullText:
Bhuvneshwar Kumar breaks silence on India comeback after R Ashwin backs him for 2027 ODI World Cup originally appeared on Cricket News. Add Cricket News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.

Bhuvneshwar Kumar says he has made peace with life outside the India team.

The comments follow Ravichandran Ashwin backing him for the 2027 World Cup.

The 36-year-old insists he now plays purely for the love of the game.

Bhuvneshwar Kumar has broken his silence on the growing clamour for an India recall, striking a notably measured tone even as pundits push his case for the 2027 ODI World Cup. The veteran seamer, whose stellar IPL 2026 campaign reignited the debate, insists he has made peace with his life away from the national team.

His remarks come days after Ravichandran Ashwin publicly backed him for a place in India's World Cup plans. Speaking on his YouTube channel, Ashwin said, "Bhuvneshwar Kumar is a yes. I would tell him to do all the tournaments - first class, the Vijay Hazare - everything. And get him ready for South Africa. I think we would require him there."

Yet Bhuvneshwar, who last played for India in 2022, made clear that another cap is no longer the force driving his career. The right-armer credited his home environment for helping him move on without bitterness, having been a mainstay of India's attack for the best part of a decade before sliding out of the reckoning.

MORE: Abhishek Sharma scores 233 in 91 balls in district match

Bhuvneshwar was candid about how he has come to terms with his exclusion. Speaking on the RCB Podcast, he said, "I am at peace, and I give credit to my family. At home, we never talk about cricket. We never talk about whether I'll get back into the Indian team, why I wasn't selected, or what went wrong. That played a big role, and there is no regret."

He acknowledged the difficulty of accepting such a transition after years as a central figure. Bhuvneshwar said, "When you're a core member of a team, everyone says: 'Team comes first.' But when you're no longer in the team, naturally you feel: 'Maybe I should still be there.'"

For all that, he framed his situation as a natural part of the sport. Bhuvneshwar said, "I understand that transitions are a part of sport. I understand that generations change. I'm not the first player to experience this, and I certainly won't be the last. Family plays a big role. I am happy being where I am."

MORE: Jasprit Bumrah ruled out of Sri Lanka Tests! Front-runners to replace the Indian pacer listed

Bhuvneshwar was clear that his motivation now stems from enjoyment rather than ambition. He said, "I've already played for India. That's not something I have to achieve now. If I get another opportunity, that's great, but I've been there. Everything I'm doing now is because of my love for the game."

He added that experience had given him a deeper appreciation of the sport's well-worn wisdom. Bhuvneshwar said, "When you're young and playing for India, you say you love the game. But only now do I actually understand phrases like 'control the controllables', 'don't overthink' and 'play for the passion of the game'. I can genuinely feel those things."

His form has certainly not dipped, having finished as the second-highest wicket-taker in IPL 2026 with 28 scalps in 16 matches at an economy of 7.95, integral to another RCB title.

MORE: Why Bhuvneshwar Kumar could make it to India's 2027 ODI World Cup squad?

There is a quiet wisdom in Bhuvneshwar's response that reflects well on him. Rather than fuel the speculation or lobby for a return, he has taken the pressure off himself, and his emphasis on peace over ambition suggests a man unlikely to be destabilised by the noise around his name.

The irony is that this contentment may be exactly what makes him a viable option. A bowler with nothing to prove, playing freely and taking wickets in bulk, is often more dangerous than one straining for recognition.

Whether the selectors share Ashwin's enthusiasm remains to be seen, but Bhuvneshwar has answered the question in the only way he sensibly could, by refusing to let it define him.

title: 6-minute solar eclipse is coming Aug. 2, 2027. Where to see it
description: The total solar eclipse will be visible in these parts of the world. See where.
fullText:
Sky gazers are gearing up for the "eclipse of the century," penciled in for August 2027.

A total solar eclipse lasting up to six minutes and 23 seconds at its peak is expected on Aug. 2, 2027, according to NASA. The total solar eclipse, in which the moon moves perfectly between the sun and Earth, effectively casting a shadow on Earth, will be one of the longest in several decades.

In comparison, the total solar eclipse on April 8, 2024, lasted four minutes and 28 seconds at its peak. The solar eclipse of 1991, however, lasted six minutes and 53 seconds. Space.com reports that the solar eclipse on Aug. 2, 2027, will be the longest eclipse totality until 2114.

The eclipse will be visible in parts of Africa, Europe and the Middle East. However, the vast majority of the United States won't have a view of it.

Here's what to know about the solar eclipse expected on Aug. 2, 2027.

Space: Two eclipses happen in August. Here's who can see them

A partial solar eclipse will be visible in parts of Maine between 5:14 and 5:19 a.m. ET on Aug. 2, 2027, according to Time and Date. Unfortunately, this may be the only view of the phenomenon in the United States.

The solar eclipse's path of totality will cross over parts of Africa, Europe and the Middle East, according to National Eclipse and NASA.

Parts of the following countries are within the path of totality.

Other countries in Africa, Europe and the Middle East will have a partial view of the eclipse.

The Aug. 2, 2027, phenomenon isn't the next total solar eclipse. On Aug. 12, 2026, a solar eclipse will be visible in Greenland, Iceland, Spain, Russia and parts of Portugal, according to NASA.

title: 2,000km, eight countries, 29 days - the fastest runner to cross the Alps
description: Ultra-runner Sophie Woods runs 2,000km across eight countries in only 29 days to break the record for completing the Via Alpina - one of the world's toughest endurance challenges.
fullText:
Ultra-runner Sophie Woods ran 2,000km across eight countries in only 29 days to break the record for completing the Via Alpina - one of the world's toughest endurance challenges.

The course follows the entire length of the Alps with elevation equivalent to climbing Mount Everest 12 times.

The 42-year-old began the marathon on 4 July in Italy, following a trail network through Slovenia, Austria, Germany, Liechtenstein, Switzerland and France before ending on the Mediterranean coast in Monaco on Saturday night.

New Zealander Woods and her team battled two heatwaves, storms, a swarm of horseflies, and wildfires that resulted in a detour that added five kilometres and 200m of treacherous climbing to her route.

British runner Jake Catterall set the previous fastest-known time for the route, completing it in 35 days in 2024.

"I am ecstatic but knackered," Woods told BBC Sport.

"The last couple of days I did on one and a half to two and a half hours of sleep to really push at the end

"That tipped me over the edge a little bit."

The Via Alpina route is considered so arduous and technical that only a handful of runners have ever attempted it under formal timing.

"There were a few points where I felt like I don't know how I'm going to get to the finish of this," she said.

"I never wanted to stop but the enormity of the task was overwhelming at times.

"I might not be the fastest person out there but I know how to do big, long days in the mountains and just keep moving when everything hurts."

Eating was key to Woods' success.

Fuelled by McDonald's, pasta and energy gels to sustain her for 15 to 18 hours of running a day, Woods was supported along the course by husband George, friend Zoe and Nila the dog.

"The first week was horrendous - everything was swollen, everything was sore. I was sure I was going to pull 15 million muscles," Woods said.

"Week two wasn't great either and then week three, I felt like I was getting fitter.

"It was like I was eating mountains for breakfast."

Several European nations have been afflicted by wildfires this summer during a succession of heatwaves.

Italy put nearly all of its major cities on the highest 'red' alert for high temperatures on Saturday, while wildfires in France, Spain and Portugal have forced more than 300,000 people to evacuate their homes.

"I've been close to wildfires before and they are terrifying. I didn't want to put myself, my crew or anyone in danger by going through the fires," Woods said.

"We had a rough plan of what it [the route] was going to look like, but there was quite a lot of winging it along the way.

"All of our calculations were out. Every day was longer and higher than we had calculated."

Woods' achievement marks an incredible year for women in ultra-running, after Rachel Entrekin won the Cocodona 250 in a record-breaking time in May.

After undergoing a gruelling fertility journey, including going through IVF, Woods says she wanted "her life to look different".

Once she decided to take up the challenge of running Via Alpina, the record was in her sights from the start.

"I didn't want to be running for more than 30 days - 30 days is enough," she said.

"I knew that I was strong and capable. But this has taken it over and beyond that.

"Ultra-running is about preparation, mental strength and being able to continue to persevere when things go wrong.

"I think women are really good at adapting and continuing."

So, what does someone who has run for 18 hours a day for 29 days straight do now?

"I intend to spend quite a lot of time on the couch and watch Netflix - and eat some vegetables," she added.
